text: The petitioner, Sri V. Venkateshulu, has approached this Court by way of writ petition WP 13296/2022 under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, challenging the proceedings initiated by the second respondent for acquisition of his agricultural land at Survey No. 47/2 in Devanahalli Taluk.

The factual matrix giving rise to the present petition is that the petitioner is the absolute owner of land measuring two acres and twenty guntas, having purchased the same under a registered sale deed dated 18.06.2007.

The Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board issued a preliminary notification dated 12.04.2014 under Section 28(1) of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, proposing to acquire the said land for the formation of an industrial area.

Pursuant to the said preliminary notification, the petitioner filed his objections on 30.05.2014 contending that his land is the only source of livelihood for his family and that several alternative parcels of vacant Government land are available in the vicinity.

After considering the objections, a final notification under Section 28(4) of the Act came to be issued on 11.11.2014, including the petitioner's land in the proposed acquisition. The petitioner's earlier writ petition challenging the said notification was disposed of on 02.03.2015 with liberty to make a fresh representation.
The petitioner thereafter submitted a representation on 21.04.2015 reiterating his earlier objections and seeking exclusion of his land from the acquisition proceedings.

Notice dated 04.08.2015 was issued by the second respondent for implementation of the rehabilitation and resettlement plan in respect of the acquired lands. The said notice was followed by an award passed under Section 29(2) of the Act on 17.12.2015 fixing the compensation at Rs. 12,40,000 per acre.

Aggrieved by the said award, the petitioner approached the reference court under Section 30 of the Act, which proceedings are stated to be still pending. The present petition is confined to the question of legality of the acquisition itself.

It is the petitioner's case that despite repeated representations, the second respondent had implemented the acquisition proceedings without affording a meaningful opportunity of hearing or considering the alternative sites suggested.

The State, in its statement of objections, has narrated that the acquisition was carried out strictly in conformity with the procedure prescribed under the 1966 Act, and that the petitioner had been heard at every stage.

Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the impugned acquisition is vitiated by non-application of mind inasmuch as the objections filed under Section 28(2) were never considered on merits, and the final notification merely repeats the contents of the preliminary notification verbatim.

Counsel further contends that the second respondent has failed to demonstrate any public purpose for the acquisition, and that the entire exercise is colourable, intended only to benefit a private industrial undertaking.

Learned Additional Advocate General appearing for the State, per contra, submits that the acquisition was carried out in compliance with every requirement of the statute, and that the petitioner's grievance is, in substance, only about the quantum of compensation, which is the subject matter of the pending reference.

Learned counsel for the second respondent adopts the submissions of the State and additionally urges that the writ petition is barred by delay and laches inasmuch as it was filed nearly seven years after the final notification.

We have heard learned counsel on both sides at length and perused the records placed before us. The principal question that arises for consideration is whether the impugned acquisition proceedings suffer from any jurisdictional infirmity warranting interference under Article 226.

On a careful examination of the objections filed by the petitioner and the order disposing of those objections, we find that the second respondent has, in fact, recorded reasons for rejecting the suggestion of alternative sites. The reasons may be brief, but they are not non-existent.

In Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, (2010) 7 SCC 129, the Supreme Court has held that the adequacy of reasons recorded while disposing of objections is a matter to be tested with reference to the statutory scheme and not in the abstract. We are of the view that the said principle is squarely attracted to the facts of the present case.

The contention that the acquisition is colourable is, in our considered view, unsustainable. The records demonstrate that the lands were acquired for the formation of an industrial estate to be administered by the Board itself, which qualifies as a public purpose under the 1966 Act.

Insofar as the plea of delay and laches is concerned, we find merit in the submission of the State. The petitioner accepted the award proceedings, participated in the reference, and only thereafter chose to question the underlying acquisition. Such conduct disentitles him to discretionary relief under Article 226.

On the totality of the circumstances, we are not persuaded that the impugned acquisition warrants interference. The petitioner's substantive grievance, if any, lies in the pending reference proceedings, where the question of compensation can be agitated on its merits.

Accordingly, while declining to interfere with the acquisition itself, we direct the second respondent to ensure that the compensation amount along with all statutory benefits is disbursed to the petitioner within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of a copy of this order, subject to the outcome of the pending reference.

The second respondent is further directed to file a compliance affidavit before the Registrar (Judicial) of this Court within four weeks of disbursement, indicating the manner and date of payment, with proof of remittance annexed thereto.

The reference court is requested to dispose of the pending reference under Section 30 of the Act expeditiously and, in any event, within a period of six months from the date of communication of this order.
Subject to the directions issued in the preceding paragraphs, the writ petition is dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs. Ordered accordingly.
